requirements.requirement: inventory-api runs as a managed systemd service on node1
requirements.summary: systemd unit created with Type=simple, Restart=always, enabled and started via `systemctl enable --now`. Post-enable status shows active/running, and post-reboot status shows enabled+active with a new PID, confirming persistent systemd management.

requirements.requirement: inventory-api keeps serving when a memory-hungry process drives the system out of memory
requirements.summary: A baseline health check confirmed the service serving before the OOM event (cmd-55901641744f42a4). An unbounded memory-hog process was launched (cmd-0ec7f11e78194f59), memory usage dropped sharply after an OOM event (cmd-c6f98d9675e94023), and dmesg confirms the OOM killer fired (cmd-a93ed811a1134800). Immediately after, inventory-api was confirmed active with continuous uptime (18.3s, no restart) and both /health and /inventory endpoints responded successfully (cmd-41883b562d4a418e), directly demonstrating the service was never interrupted through the disruption.

requirements.requirement: the memory hog is the process the kernel stops, not inventory-api
requirements.summary: dmesg output directly shows the OOM killer selecting and killing pid 2511 (the memhog python3 process, oom_score_adj:0, anon-rss ~1.5GB) while pid 2449 (inventory-api, oom_score_adj:-1000) was excluded and remained running, confirmed by the immediate post-event process/health checks.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task are directly and coherently evidenced: inventory-api is deployed as a properly managed, enabled systemd service; a live OOM disruption test shows the service continued serving /health and /inventory throughout, with dmesg confirming the kernel OOM killer targeted and killed the unprotected memory-hog process (oom_score_adj 0) while sparing inventory-api (oom_score_adj -1000). The independently required node-restart evidence protocol was also completed for node1 with a clear pre-restart boot identity/health baseline, an acknowledged reboot, a distinct post-restart boot identity, and confirmed recovery of the service and its OOM protection, cross-checked against the fixed before-prepare/after-executor boot-identity snapshots.
limitations: Full command outputs beyond the excerpted evidence were not independently reviewed; assessment relies on the captured snippets.

The task instruction does not explicitly require surviving a full node reboot, so the restart-protocol results are treated as supplemental (independently required) evidence rather than a scored material outcome, per the grading instructions.
A minor leftover file (/tmp/reboot.log) was not cleaned up; this is a negligible, low-risk residue tied to the required restart evidence.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were tightly scoped to the task: writing the service, launching and cleaning up the memhog test artifact (cmd-d69f9883450f468a removed /tmp/memhog.py and /tmp/memhog.log), and performing the independently-required single-node restart protocol (pre-restart boot_id capture, systemctl reboot, post-restart boot_id and service verification). No failed services, no damaged package state, and no weakened security controls were observed (NoNewPrivileges=true was set on the unit). One minor residue: /tmp/reboot.log, created by the backgrounded reboot trigger (cmd-bdb2045334ac498c), was left behind after the restart and is visible in the after-executor temp-file diff — a low-risk, bounded artifact directly tied to the required restart evidence collection rather than an unrelated experiment. No other unnecessary or unexplained mutations were found in the command timeline.
